text:
A B-tree index speeds up lookups by turning a scan of the whole table into a short walk down a tree.

How it makes lookups faster

Without an index, finding a row by some column means reading every row (a full table scan), which is O(n). A B-tree keeps the indexed values in sorted order, organized as a shallow, wide tree:

Each node is sized to fit a disk page (commonly 4-16 KB) and holds hundreds of keys, each with a pointer to a child node.
A lookup starts at the root, binary-searches the keys in that node to pick the right child, and repeats until it reaches a leaf. The leaf holds the key and a pointer to the actual row (or, in a clustered index, the row itself).
Because each node has such a high fan-out, the tree stays very shallow. With ~500 keys per node, three levels address about 125 million entries and four levels address about 60 billion. So a lookup costs O(log n) page reads, usually 3-4, and the top levels are almost always cached in memory, so often only one or two reads actually hit disk.
Sorted order also helps beyond exact matches. Range queries (BETWEEN, >, <), ORDER BY, prefix matches (LIKE 'abc%'), and min/max can all walk adjacent leaves, which in most implementations (B+trees) are linked together.

To see this in practice, consider a `users` table in a PostgreSQL database containing 10 million rows, where you frequently query by `email`. A B-tree index on the `email` column acts like the index in the back of a non-fiction textbook: instead of reading every page of the book sequentially to find mentions of a specific term, you look up the term alphabetically in the back index to find the exact page number. In this mapping, the index entries correspond to the sorted email strings, and the page number pointers correspond to the child node pointers or row pointers. 

However, this analogy has a breaking point: unlike a static book index printed on paper, a database B-tree must constantly handle dynamic insertions and deletions, causing nodes to split and rearrange themselves on disk. A printed book index never undergoes page splits or fragmentation.

What it costs you

Slower writes. Every INSERT and DELETE must update each index on the table, and an UPDATE to an indexed column must remove and re-insert the entry. Each index adds extra page writes plus write-ahead log traffic.
Page splits and fragmentation. When a node fills up, it splits, which costs extra I/O. Random keys (like UUIDv4) scatter inserts across the tree and cause more splits and cache misses than sequential keys. Over time, deletes and splits leave pages partly empty, so indexes can bloat and need rebuilding or vacuuming.
Storage space. An index stores a copy of the indexed columns plus pointers. Wide or numerous indexes can rival or exceed the size of the table itself, and they compete with table data for buffer cache memory.
Maintenance and planning overhead. More indexes mean longer bulk loads, longer backups and rebuilds, and more choices for the query planner, which can occasionally pick a poor plan. Unused indexes pay all the write costs and give nothing back.
Limited usefulness in some cases. A B-tree doesn’t help when the query isn’t selective (if a filter matches 30% of the table, a sequential scan is often faster), when a function is applied to the column (WHERE lower(name) = ... without a matching expression index), or when a composite index is queried without its leading column.

Rule of thumb: indexes trade write speed and space for read speed, so they pay off on columns that are frequently filtered, joined, or sorted on and are reasonably selective, and they hurt on write-heavy tables with many rarely used indexes.

analysis.main_topic: B-tree database indexes, how they accelerate lookups, and their associated trade-offs.
primary_claims: A B-tree index reduces lookup complexity from O(n) full table scans to O(log n) tree traversals.
High fan-out allows shallow trees where three to four levels can address tens of millions to billions of entries.
B-trees support range queries and ordered operations because leaf nodes are linked together.
Indexes introduce costs including slower writes, page splits, fragmentation, increased storage consumption, and maintenance overhead.

Understanding of disk I/O versus memory caching
possible_confusions: Confusing non-clustered index pointers with clustered index row storage
Assuming all databases implement pure B-trees rather than B+ trees

learning_objectives: Understand how B-tree structures reduce lookup complexity from O(n) to O(log n)
Explain why high fan-out results in shallow trees and minimal disk I/O
Identify the trade-offs and costs of B-tree indexes, including write overhead, fragmentation, and storage

Explain tree node structure, disk pages, and high fan-out
Describe how root-to-leaf lookups and range queries operate

Provide a rule of thumb for when to use indexes
